newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - Australian authorities hit back over gold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Australian authorities hit back over gold.

text.p: The Australian government and its central bank lashed back on Friday at critics of the bank's sale of two thirds of its gold, arguing that speculators and gold miners themselves were to blame for this year's price slump.

Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer said "24 year-old screen jockeys with braces" in the world's financial markets had to accept more responsibility for the fall in the price of gold to 12-year lows this week.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) announced last week it had sold 167 tonnes of gold over the past six months, spooking a gold market already nervous about central bank sales into panic selling that cut the price 6.5 percent.

The RBA said there was no reason for the central bank of a gold-rich country like Australia to hold large gold reserves and the money tied up in the precious metal had been put to better use buying foreign securities like bonds.

Local gold miners and the World Gold Council savaged the central bank sell-off, saying it was insensitive, shortsighted and virtually unpatriotic. It would also render many Australian gold mines uneconomic.
One miner even suggested it was time to reconsider the bank's independence.
Fischer, whose government sanctioned the sale before it took place, said it was unfair to blame Canberra as the gold price was set by traders around world.

"If they've got to close out or hedge with pain the speculative positions they've taken, I'm not going to shed one tear for them," Fischer told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio in South Africa where he is on a trade mission.
South Africa and Australia are the world's first and third largest gold producers respectively.
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane, in his first media interview since his appointment last year, also went on the defensive after a week of criticism over the gold sell-off.
He said the miners themselves had not helped the price by pursuing big hedging programmes and by keeping the issue alive in the media.

Macfarlane told The Australian newspaper the mining industry "is not helping the price by keeping these issues in the headlines every day," adding: "Heavy forward selling by producers has not helped either."
Macfarlane said the bank often had to take decisions in the national interest which hurt sectoral groups.
"If we raise interest rates, the housing sector is the first to complain; if the exchange rate rises, it's usually the farmers and miners. We have to live with this," he said.
"I think they (miners) somewhat exaggerate our impact on the overall world market," Macfarlane was quoted as saying.
He said the gold price had been heavily influenced over the past year by European central bank sales and by proposals by the International Monetary Fund to sell gold to fund debt relief.
He also cited a research paper from the U.S. Federal Reserve proposing that the U.S. central bank sell down its reserves.
